articles.summary: Fine-tuning a generator on a complete high-resolution canvas requires long image sequences and substantial computation, yet local regions can still exhibit unnatural repetitive stripes when training…
articles.abstract: Fine-tuning a generator on a complete high-resolution canvas requires long image sequences and substantial computation, yet local regions can still exhibit unnatural repetitive stripes when training resources are limited. We introduce Qwen-Image-HD, which adapts Qwen-Image 2.0 to high-resolution synthesis through local training and blockwise autoregressive generation. Each prediction covers a target tile at 1K scale, conditioned on high-resolution upper and left neighbors and a compressed historical thumbnail. These conditions provide adjacent fine-scale structures and an overview of the scene generated so far. To integrate these complementary cues, we map both forms of history and the target to a shared canvas coordinate system to express their spatial relationships and scale differences. On Qwen-Image-Bench at 4K, Qwen-Image-HD achieves stronger overall evaluation performance than direct 4K generation with FLUX-3-Image-Klein. Compared with full-image 4K supervised fine-tuning of the same backbone, it achieves better generation quality with lower training compute and higher inference efficiency, while exhibiting fewer unnatural repetitive stripes in original-resolution comparisons. We further introduce a Wavefront-AutoRegressive inference schedule that generates tiles on the same anti-diagonal concurrently across GPUs to reduce single-image latency.

articles.title: Reinforcing Diffusion Models by Instantaneous Trajectory Distribution Matching
articles.summary: Forward diffusion reinforcement learning (RL)---enabling deterministic ODE sampling without trajectory backpropagation---has grown increasingly popular for efficiently aligning diffusion models.…
articles.abstract: Forward diffusion reinforcement learning (RL)---enabling deterministic ODE sampling without trajectory backpropagation---has grown increasingly popular for efficiently aligning diffusion models. However, we reveal that existing methods essentially rely on signed reward-weighted regression (RWR), regressing the trainable policy velocity onto rollouts from a behavior distribution. Unbiased baseline subtraction implicitly assumes that the policy velocity equals the behavior marginal velocity---an idealized assumption violated under classifier-free guidance (CFG) rollouts, offline/off-policy updates, and imperfect online self-consistency. This behavior--policy mismatch breaks baseline invariance and injects baseline-induced gradient drift, destabilizing training. To resolve this issue, we propose Instantaneous Trajectory Distribution Matching (iTDM), taking the infinitesimal limit of Trajectory Distribution Matching toward a time-local reward-guided target via the posterior-score identity to yield a sample-level gradient anchored at the behavior velocity without learning an additional reward-tilted target score. Tracking this velocity with an online auxiliary denoiser guarantees exact baseline invariance at the auxiliary optimum, effectively suppressing baseline drift across both online and offline RL. Extensive experiments across compositional generation, text rendering, and preference alignment show that iTDM achieves state-of-the-art in-domain and out-of-domain performance across group-wise online/offline RL and pairwise offline RL. Notably, on the challenging GenEval2 benchmark, iTDM converges nearly 3\times faster than competing methods while scaling smoothly to 0.87 without collapse. Furthermore, iTDM scales effectively to the 5.6B FLUX.3 model, achieving better performance across both in-domain and unseen metrics. Code is available at https://github.com/Luo-Yihong/iTDM

articles.title: SpecEngineeringBench: Evaluating Coding Agents as Autonomous Specification Engineers
articles.summary: Autonomous specification engineering requires coding agents to translate functional requirements into executable tests and use the results to discover and validate defects. However, existing…
articles.abstract: Autonomous specification engineering requires coding agents to translate functional requirements into executable tests and use the results to discover and validate defects. However, existing benchmarks evaluate coding agents on explicitly specified test generation tasks, commonly providing an issue description, a designated test entry point, or files to inspect, leaving the ability to determine what to test and where to investigate insufficiently evaluated. Relying on such clues bypasses the challenge of mapping requirements to implementations and proactively uncovering unknown defects. We propose SpecEngineeringBench, comprising 100 instances from 78 open-source Python repositories across 16 application categories, with multiple recorded defects in each instance. Two independent tasks evaluate complementary capabilities: generating test suites and discovering defects through execution analysis. The evaluation combines test validity, defect detection, and coverage with localization precision and recall. Across seven frontier coding agents, results reveal that test validity and coverage decouple from defect exposure: agents achieve a 91.47% Head Pass Rate and 80.48% Change-focused Coverage alongside a 26.36% Fail-to-Pass Rate, while localization recall drops from 78.11% at the file level to 51.29% at the function level. Autonomous test generation improves file, function, and hunk localization recall by 4.99, 2.77, and 2.69 percentage points over relying solely on existing repository test suites.

articles.title: Coding4Games: Can Modern Coding Agents Play Modern Video Games?
articles.summary: Games, especially modern AAA games, challenge language models to perceive complex scenes, control actions, and make decisions over long horizons. Existing game benchmarks primarily test language…
articles.abstract: Games, especially modern AAA games, challenge language models to perceive complex scenes, control actions, and make decisions over long horizons. Existing game benchmarks primarily test language models as computer-use agents that query a language model throughout play, incurring repeated inference cost and, in real-time games, acting while the environment continues to evolve. We ask whether coding agents can learn from game interaction to develop standalone game-playing programs that run without language model inference. We thus introduce Coding4Games, a benchmark for evaluating whether coding agents can develop standalone programs that play modern games through visual observations and standard game inputs. Coding4Games has three defining features: 1) Diverse Modern Games, covering 15 games with diverse visual, strategic, and control demands; 2) Development-Test Separation, in which a coding agent uses a sandbox and the standard player interface to iteratively develop a program, after which the selected program is frozen and independently tested without language-model inference; and 3) Outcome and Process Evaluation, which measures not only game performance and reliability but also how agents use feedback, revise programs, and resolve problems during development. Across 15 games, the best program per game outscores the strongest GUI baseline on 13 and ties it on one. The human player outscores all agents on 10 games. We additionally examine the effects of development budgets. Coding4Games evaluates whether coding agents can turn their understanding of complex interactive environments into programs that work reliably on their own.

articles.title: VenusOCR2.0: Towards Efficient and Effective Document Parsing
articles.summary: We present VenusOCR2.0, a compact 1B-parameter vision-language recognizer designed for both high-accuracy and high-throughput document parsing across text, tables, and formulas. To continuously…
articles.abstract: We present VenusOCR2.0, a compact 1B-parameter vision-language recognizer designed for both high-accuracy and high-throughput document parsing across text, tables, and formulas. To continuously improve recognition quality without self-training collapse, we build a bounded recursive self-improvement (RSI) data engine where the model acts strictly as a weakness probe, while external multi-expert medoid consensus, VLM visual verification, and factorized synthesis supply reliable supervision across pretraining, curated SFT, and RLVR. VenusOCR2.0 couples a dynamic-resolution SigLIP2 encoder and 2x2 spatial token merging with a Qwen3-0.6B decoder, adopting compact atomic OTSL tokens to shorten table sequences and reduce structural errors. To further eliminate the autoregressive decoding bottleneck, we introduce PTPv2, a lightweight (sim67M) decoupled parallel draft module that combines frozen multi-layer verifier conditioning, a standalone learned mask, and block-causal all-position next-token prediction. On OmniDocBenchv1.6, VenusOCR2.0 achieves an overall score of 96.45 and a state-of-the-art 98.57 formula CDM, substantially outperforming massive general-purpose VLMs such as Gemini-3-Pro (92.91) and Qwen3-VL-235B (89.78). Deployed in vLLM on a single H20 GPU, PTPv2 delivers a 2.96x single-request speedup and up to 2.36x higher batched throughput while guaranteeing lossless, token-for-token equivalence with standard autoregressive decoding.

articles.title: LoopDVR: Looped Transformer for Efficient Dense Visual Recognition
articles.summary: We propose LoopDVR, a framework for converting pretrained Transformer-based dense visual recognition models into parameter-efficient looped networks. Rather than reducing the network width or depth…
articles.abstract: We propose LoopDVR, a framework for converting pretrained Transformer-based dense visual recognition models into parameter-efficient looped networks. Rather than reducing the network width or depth directly, LoopDVR reuses Transformer blocks across layers in both the ViT backbone and Transformer decoder, reducing the number of parameters while retaining the original computational structure. However, naively sharing parameters can disrupt the distinct transformations learned at different depths. To address this challenge, we identify suitable sharing groups based on inter-layer representation dissimilarity and keep the final backbone block independent for multi-scale feature construction. We then initialize each shared backbone block with the pretrained weights of its group's terminal layer to better preserve the learned representations. An independent Loop Adapter at each layer further helps retain depth-specific transformations within shared blocks. Subsequently, we distill visual representations into the looped backbone and integrate it with a looped decoder for task-specific training. Experiments demonstrate that LoopDVR achieves the best accuracy--parameter trade-offs across dense recognition tasks. Compared with the reference models, it reduces parameters by approximately 28% while maintaining competitive accuracy. Notably, LoopDet-S achieves 50.9 box AP with only 7.0M parameters, highlighting its effectiveness in compact models.

articles.title: Residual Guidance for Real-Time Interactive Video Generation
articles.summary: Real-time interactive video generation allows users to change the prompt during generation to steer the evolving video. However, existing streaming models, which generate videos chunk by chunk, often…
articles.abstract: Real-time interactive video generation allows users to change the prompt during generation to steer the evolving video. However, existing streaming models, which generate videos chunk by chunk, often keep following the previous prompt after a switch. We trace this failure to context inertia, where the previous chunk acts as a strong prior that suppresses the new prompt. Furthermore, we find that this inertia persists even when the cache retains only the previous chunk, yet discarding the context breaks visual continuity, which limits approaches that edit the cache. Rather than editing the cache, we propose Residual Guidance (RG), a simple, training-free method that counteracts context inertia with a correction measured outside the cache. Specifically, RG denoises the re-noised previous chunk once under the new prompt without the cache and adds the resulting residual to the early denoising steps of the next chunk, where its content is largely decided and the new prompt is most suppressed. Across settings ranging from a single switch to long multi-switch generation, RG substantially improves prompt switching capability on existing streaming models, including those with dedicated switching mechanisms, while largely retaining visual quality. As it requires no training or per-model tuning and adds only one forward pass per chunk, RG can be easily integrated into existing real-time video generation pipelines.

articles.title: Separating Measurement Failures from Defence Failures in Split Language-Model Privacy
articles.summary: Split-training privacy evaluations fail through distinct mechanisms. Evaluators can overlook an exposed gradient channel, align reconstructions against shifted labels, or deploy uncalibrated probes…
articles.abstract: Split-training privacy evaluations fail through distinct mechanisms. Evaluators can overlook an exposed gradient channel, align reconstructions against shifted labels, or deploy uncalibrated probes before testing a candidate defence, while calibrated attacks can also refute real defences. Separating these failure modes alters which claims survive. We conduct a retrospective evidentiary reanalysis across four split-LLM campaigns and two cross-cutting scope checks covering host key custody and variational mutual-information bounds, mapping every recorded claim to one of five admissibility states (breach, non-detection, undetermined coverage, invalid measurement, or out-of-scope inference). Across a 19-configuration exploration, only four of 24 required probes qualified, yet those four calibrated probes still established qualified privacy breaches in 13 configurations, while utility or learning-gain failures eliminated the remaining 6. In a seven-cell defence-redesign pilot, 2 quantised configurations failed utility gates, calibrated next-byte structure probes breached the 0.02 gate on all 7 cells (0.097 to 0.112), and qualified punctuation-property probes reached 0.79 to 0.89, yielding 4 failed and 3 undetermined composite privacy assessments (the latter from marginal null-band excursions on punctuation bindings). Negative evidence against both defence families remains intact. Scope checks further show that shared-key orthogonal wrappers protect passive network captures without hiding activations from a compromised restoring host, and why near-zero variational lower bounds leave worst-case leakage unconstrained. Rerunnable scripts verify 1,522 checks across 122 SHA-256-pinned artifacts while preserving each campaign's native seed intervals and retrospective boundaries.

articles.title: Distill to Loop: Turning Pretrained Diffusion Transformers into Looped Models with Adjustable Depth
articles.summary: Looped transformers reuse one block of shared weights along the depth of the network. Recent looped diffusion transformers are trained from scratch, which repeats the full pretraining cost although…
articles.abstract: Looped transformers reuse one block of shared weights along the depth of the network. Recent looped diffusion transformers are trained from scratch, which repeats the full pretraining cost although strong pretrained non-looped diffusion transformers exist. We propose Distill to Loop (Dooop), which distills a pretrained non-looped diffusion transformer into a looped student whose blocks are initialized from the teacher's. We cast distillation as a fixed-point iteration toward the teacher, in which the output after every loop is trained toward the teacher, and each loop is one step of an ordinary differential equation in depth. As a result, one model runs any number of loops at test time without retraining, and the higher-order ODE solvers of diffusion model sampling can be applied along the depth dimension for better results. Meanwhile, because a looped model produces an output after every loop, we also construct loop guidance between the outputs of different loop counts, which improves the generated samples at little extra compute. On SD3-medium, a looped student with about 37% of the teacher's parameters matches the teacher on average over GenEval, ImageReward, PickScore and HPSv2.1 with two to four loops, and with two loops it uses about 58% of the teacher's compute. And on a four-step SD3-medium, loop guidance raises the average of the four metrics from 88.2 to 99.2.

articles.title: GRAPE-Bench: When Vision Degrades, Does Video Reasoning Hold?
articles.summary: Despite strong performance on standard benchmarks, video reasoning models remain vulnerable to visual degradation, raising concerns about their reliability in safety-critical scenarios. Existing…
articles.abstract: Despite strong performance on standard benchmarks, video reasoning models remain vulnerable to visual degradation, raising concerns about their reliability in safety-critical scenarios. Existing benchmarks address this concern in part by simulating visual degradation or probing model reasoning with challenging questions, leaving open how well models handle naturally degraded video and whether they can make the simpler judgments that matter for safe driving. To this end, we introduce GRAPE-Bench, which jointly evaluates video reasoning across visual degradation conditions and question difficulty. It combines a synthetic set spanning twelve corruption types across daily-life and driving videos with real-world footage of driving at night or in rain, snow, or fog. Each video is paired with three progressively challenging questions, from fundamental judgments with potential safety implications to demanding reasoning stress tests. Across open-weight and frontier models, we observe ranking reversals between synthetic and real-world conditions and level-specific weaknesses obscured by overall accuracy. Synthetic-data fine-tuning improves Qwen3.5-9B's real-world accuracy from 76.7% to 81.1%, while clean-privileged on-policy distillation reaches 80.4% in a separate reasoning-enabled setting. Through preference steering, we further demonstrate continuous control over a frozen model's trade-off between safety-relevant judgments and challenging reasoning, with little change in overall accuracy. Together, GRAPE-Bench provides a unified testbed for evaluating, improving, and controlling video reasoning under degraded visual conditions.

articles.title: Clinical3D-Bench: Evaluating and Improving Spatial Intelligence of Multimodal LLMs in Hospital Environments
articles.summary: Spatial reasoning in hospitals requires tracking look-alike equipment, interpreting patient-relative directions, and judging passage widths, yet existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of these…
articles.abstract: Spatial reasoning in hospitals requires tracking look-alike equipment, interpreting patient-relative directions, and judging passage widths, yet existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of these abilities. We introduce Clinical3D-Bench, a simulated benchmark with 3,368 questions of eight types on egocentric walkthroughs of 373 hospital-room layouts. Layouts follow hospital design guidelines, answers are computed from the 3D scenes, and paired scene states test whether models change their answers when relevant evidence changes. Videos are photorealistic, and ten physicians screened the layouts. Among 35 multimodal large language models (MLLMs), the best open and proprietary models reach 45.7% and 53.6% macro accuracy, against 40.8% for an answer prior and 79.0% for physicians on a subset, and 27 of 32 open models score below 40% on two-way patient-relative directions. Fine-tuning on Clinical3D-45K, our 44,750-question training set, lifts two MLLMs 16-20 points above the best proprietary model. 3D maps given to the fine-tuned MLLM as input go largely unused: replacing them with another video's, even when they are ground truth, barely changes its accuracy. The proposed GeoJeV instead lets the MLLM compute with 3D: it reconstructs a scene memory from each video, selects 3D operations and their arguments from the MLLM's question state, and adds their evidence to its option scores. It achieves the highest accuracy of all evaluated models, narrowing the gap to physicians.

articles.title: SpatialArena: Where Do Geometric Foundation Models Stand?
articles.summary: 3D perception is shifting from task-specific pipelines to geometric foundation models: monocular depth networks, feed-forward 3D/4D reconstruction models, and vision--language models that predict…
articles.abstract: 3D perception is shifting from task-specific pipelines to geometric foundation models: monocular depth networks, feed-forward 3D/4D reconstruction models, and vision--language models that predict geometry. However, their progress cannot be measured reliably. Published numbers are not comparable, because every paper samples frames, sets resolutions, and selects test splits differently. They are not robust because the alignment required for every up-to-scale prediction can outweigh the gap between models: fitting depth in the wrong space nearly triples its error, and standard trajectory alignment understates the error of failing methods by up to 2.6times. And they rarely cover long recordings, dynamic scenes, or aerial views. We present SpatialArena, an open arena that scores geometric models with the same metrics and rules, with robust and deterministic alignment. SpatialArena spans five tasks, from monocular depth to SLAM. It covers 23 public datasets with 418,929 images across indoor, outdoor, aerial, object-centric, and dynamic scenes, together with Spatial Arena, our own captures with accurate poses and depth. Evaluating 52 models, we find that single-image depth is close to saturation on public benchmarks but not on large, uncontrolled scenes, and that progress now comes from consistency across frames and views, where feed-forward 3D/4D models match or surpass monocular specialists and overtake video depth models. The benchmark, toolbox, and leaderboard will be publicly released.

articles.title: Online Statistical Inference for Derivative-Free Constrained Stochastic Optimization
articles.summary: We study statistical inference for nonlinear equality-constrained stochastic optimization problems in settings where derivative information is unavailable or expensive to obtain. While recent…
articles.abstract: We study statistical inference for nonlinear equality-constrained stochastic optimization problems in settings where derivative information is unavailable or expensive to obtain. While recent advances in stochastic sequential quadratic programming (SSQP) have enabled efficient online optimization, existing methods either rely on gradient information or suffer from high computational costs. To address these limitations, we develop a sketched derivative-free SSQP (SDF-SSQP) method that simultaneously achieves computational efficiency and valid statistical inference. By leveraging randomized sketching, the proposed method reduces the per-iteration computational cost to $O((d+m)^2)$, where $d$ is the dimension of the decision variable and $m$ is the number of constraints, making it well suited for large-scale problems. To overcome the challenges that both sketching and zeroth-order approximations introduce for statistical inference, we adopt a random-scaling approach that eliminates the need for explicit estimation of the asymptotic covariance matrix. We establish the asymptotic normality of the averaged primal--dual iterates and construct a self-normalized statistic that is asymptotically pivotal. The resulting inference procedure is fully online, requires neither covariance estimation nor matrix inversion, and incurs an additional per-iteration cost of the same order as that of the optimization update. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in terms of both optimization performance and statistical inference accuracy.

articles.title: A Kernel Framework for Linear Operator Equations
articles.summary: Solving linear operator equations with nonlocal terms or heterogeneous constraints often requires specific numerical schemes. We develop a unified approach based on embedding such equations into a…
articles.abstract: Solving linear operator equations with nonlocal terms or heterogeneous constraints often requires specific numerical schemes. We develop a unified approach based on embedding such equations into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). Differential, boundary, and integral operators are represented by their Riesz representers in the RKHS. The equations are solved in the regularized least-squares sense at finitely many collocation points. The solution is a finite linear combination of operator-induced representers and is obtained from a single linear system. Its sensitivities, such as financial Greeks, follow by direct differentiation. To reduce the computational cost for large collocation sets, we introduce a Nyström approximation based on subsampling the operator-induced representers. It yields the best approximation of this solution within the reduced trial space, in a regularized empirical norm. Numerical examples cover ordinary, partial, and partial integro-differential equations, including multi-asset and jump-diffusion option pricing.

articles.title: Bayesian Data Integration and Model Updating in Probabilistic Digital Twins
articles.summary: This paper proposes a framework for sequential Bayesian updating in probabilistic digital twins using data from multiple sources collected over time. The framework distinguishes between property data…
articles.abstract: This paper proposes a framework for sequential Bayesian updating in probabilistic digital twins using data from multiple sources collected over time. The framework distinguishes between property data and behavior data, according to how observations relate to the digital state. Property data directly inform a subset of the uncertain model parameters and can therefore be incorporated using efficient dedicated Bayesian updating methods. Behavior data provide indirect information through the prediction model and require the solution of a Bayesian inverse problem. To reduce the associated computational cost, an active-learning-based surrogate strategy is introduced that evolves with the digital state and adaptively refines the prediction model in regions relevant to posterior inference. The framework is evaluated using an idealized cantilever beam example and a geotechnical case study of a canal wall subject to varying water levels and corrosion. The examples show how complementary data sources, including both equality observations and inequality information from observed system survival, can inform uncertain parameters and system reliability. The proposed surrogate-based updating scheme yields posterior estimates and prediction accuracy comparable to those of physics-based updating while requiring substantially fewer model evaluations. The proposed framework thus supports multi-source updating and reliability assessment in probabilistic digital twins of engineering systems.

articles.title: Instance-Dependent Bandit Convex Optimization in One Dimension
articles.summary: We study the instance-dependent sample complexity of one-dimensional stochastic bandit convex optimization in the fixed-confidence setting. First, we consider minimizer localization, where the…
articles.abstract: We study the instance-dependent sample complexity of one-dimensional stochastic bandit convex optimization in the fixed-confidence setting. First, we consider minimizer localization, where the learner seeks to identify a point within distance $\varepsilon$ of the unique minimizer. We introduce a new instance-dependent quantity $Δ_\varepsilon(f)$, corresponding to the threshold for which the sublevel set of $f-\min f$ has length $2\varepsilon$. We prove a lower bound of order $Δ_\varepsilon(f)^{-2}$ and give a bisection-style algorithm that matches this rate up to logarithmic factors. We then revisit the simple-regret setting, where the goal is to identify an $\varepsilon$-optimal point. Surprisingly, no comparable instance-dependent improvement is possible: every correct algorithm has sample complexity of order $\varepsilon^{-2}$ on every instance, matching the minimax rate up to constants. Together, these results separate the statistical complexity of minimizer localization from that of simple-regret optimization in one-dimensional convex bandits.

articles.title: ExitLUT: Boolean Early Exits for Efficient FPGA-Based Neural Network Inference
articles.summary: Early exit neural networks reduce average inference cost by terminating once sufficient confidence is reached. On FPGAs, conventional confidence-based exits add arithmetic control paths poorly…
articles.abstract: Early exit neural networks reduce average inference cost by terminating once sufficient confidence is reached. On FPGAs, conventional confidence-based exits add arithmetic control paths poorly matched to LUT fabrics, consuming resources that could otherwise support the main datapath. We present ExitLUT, which replaces softmax-style exit decisions with learned Boolean functions mapped directly into FPGA LUTs. In our CNN evaluation, fpgaConvNet is the static spatial-dataflow baseline, while ATHEENA is its softmax-based early exit extension. ExitLUT reduces ATHEENA's exit-decision LUT usage by 2.58$\times$ over the softmax path and eliminates decision-path DSP usage, while preserving accuracy and exit behavior. Rerunning design-space exploration reinvests these savings into the datapath, improving throughput by up to 4.08$\times$ over fpgaConvNet and 1.82$\times$ over ATHEENA. For LUT-based NNs, embedded ExitLUT exits achieve 1.41-1.89$\times$ average time-to-decision speedup over static NeuraLUT-Assemble designs with under 1% LUT overhead.

articles.title: Diagnosing Epistemic Uncertainty in Neural Operators: Effects of Initialization, Discretization, and Function Sampling
articles.summary: Neural operators provide efficient surrogates for mappings between function spaces, but their reliability cannot be characterized by the performance of a single trained model. Existing neural…
articles.abstract: Neural operators provide efficient surrogates for mappings between function spaces, but their reliability cannot be characterized by the performance of a single trained model. Existing neural operator uncertainty quantification approaches often characterize predictive uncertainty without separately identifying the contributions of individual sources of epistemic uncertainty. Finite sampling of the training function space, output discretization, and model initialization can produce substantial variation among learned operators even when the underlying physical problem is deterministic. We systematically investigate these sources of epistemic uncertainty across a diverse set of operator learning architectures. Across our experiments, we train approximately 46,000 neural operator models and construct ensembles over training datasets, model initializations, and output discretizations to characterize distributions of relative $L_2$ error rather than individual trained realizations. We find substantial architecture-dependent differences in epistemic uncertainty, with model initialization often accounting for the largest proportion of variance in relative $L_2$ error. The ranked performance of neural operator architectures can invert as the number and spatial distribution of output samples change, with the best architectures under sparse or randomly sampled observations differing from those at higher-resolution or structured discretizations. Furthermore, ensembles that reliably characterize aggregate operator error can provide unreliable estimates of error quantiles for individual test functions. These results highlight the importance of distinguishing the sources of epistemic uncertainty when evaluating neural operator reliability and establishing robust benchmarking practices.

articles.title: SOTS: Signature-based Optimal Transport Selection
articles.summary: Training data selection for machine learning models is a critical bottleneck in industrial applications where expert annotation is costly and time-consuming. Existing coreset selection methods for…
articles.abstract: Training data selection for machine learning models is a critical bottleneck in industrial applications where expert annotation is costly and time-consuming. Existing coreset selection methods for time series either ignore temporal structure entirely or cannot handle variable-length, irregularly sampled, multi-channel signals, the setting most common in industrial monitoring and testing. We introduce SOTS (Signature-based Optimal Transport Selection), an unsupervised coreset selection framework for irregular multivariate time series (IMTS) classification. Each sample is mapped to a truncated path signature, capturing the joint geometric structure of its channels, and the coreset is selected by greedily minimizing the Sliced Wasserstein distance between the empirical signature distributions of the candidate subset and the full dataset, a criterion for which we establish a convergence guarantee for random coresets. We validate SOTS on a real-world, highly imbalanced industrial I&C testing dataset, where SOTS-Greedy exceeds 95% of full-dataset accuracy using only 30% of the training data, outperforming standard coreset baselines at most budgets. This advantage generalizes to public UEA regular multivariate time series benchmarks specifically when class-discriminative information is purely geometric.

articles.title: Transformers with Signatures: Towards Universal In-Context Learning in Path Space
articles.summary: In-context learning (ICL) enables transformers to adapt to new tasks from demonstrations without updating their parameters. However, theoretical guarantees for transformers remain limited in general,…
articles.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) enables transformers to adapt to new tasks from demonstrations without updating their parameters. However, theoretical guarantees for transformers remain limited in general, and elusive in particular when target responses depend nonlinearly on the evolution of observed paths. We establish an ICL framework for path space, using path signature features. Building on the universal linear approximation property of signatures, we construct explicitly a causal softmax transformer with two attention heads per layer that emulates in-context Lasso. Under sparse signature approximation and suitable moment and concentration conditions, we establish finite-sample prediction error bounds. Our analysis goes beyond the IID data setting in the existing ICL theory, allowing dependence among demonstrations and the query. Experiments on in-context sparse recovery, nonlinear path regression, execution-cost prediction, and financial payoff inference demonstrate robustness to changes in observation grids and adaptation to unseen market environments. Across these prediction tasks, transformers with signatures match or outperform vanilla transformer baselines with substantially fewer trainable parameters, highlighting the effectiveness and efficiency of signature-based ICL.

articles.title: AlphaDefect: Expert-Level AI for Slay the Spire 2
articles.summary: Slay the Spire 2 (STS2) is a single-player deck-building game that requires long-term planning under heavy randomness. We present AlphaDefect, an expert-level AI system for STS2: for each character,…
articles.abstract: Slay the Spire 2 (STS2) is a single-player deck-building game that requires long-term planning under heavy randomness. We present AlphaDefect, an expert-level AI system for STS2: for each character, one network trained with proximal policy optimization (PPO) makes every decision of a run, in combat and outside it. At the highest difficulty, Ascension 10, on two versions of the game current in November 2026 and on test seeds not played in training, AlphaDefect wins 62-77% of runs across six characters with greedy play and 68-80% with test-time search, after 1.3 to 6.7 billion decisions of training per character; runs uploaded by human players of all levels are won 11-20% of the time at the same difficulty. The networks read the game as entity records that identify each card, relic and enemy through a learned embedding and attributes from the game data, together with consequences of public information computed by the engine. Ablations show how much the agent depends on this encoding: without these identities, the network did not win a single run, and without the computed consequences it won 8.3 points fewer. To our knowledge, AlphaDefect is the strongest publicly reported STS2 agent as of November 2026.

articles.title: RoFE: Rotated Frozen Embeddings for Low-Data Multimodal Tabular Learning
articles.summary: Multimodal tabular learning combines tabular data with images and text, often in settings where labeled data are scarce. Tabular foundation models such as prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) offer a…
articles.abstract: Multimodal tabular learning combines tabular data with images and text, often in settings where labeled data are scarce. Tabular foundation models such as prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) offer a promising solution via in-context learning without task-specific training. However, modern image and text encoders produce embeddings with hundreds or thousands of dimensions, far exceeding the number of features encountered during PFN pretraining. Existing approaches bridge this gap using principal component analysis (PCA) to compress frozen embeddings. Surprisingly, we find that this PCA interface can underperform simple linear classifiers when labeled examples are scarce, even though PFNs are designed for small datasets. We identify the underlying failure mechanism: the PFN's per-column standardization removes the variances of the PCA scores. When the PCA keeps every direction of the labeled examples, the examples collapse into a regular simplex in which all pairwise distances are equal. To address this problem, we propose Rotated Frozen Embeddings (RoFE), a training-free method that rotates PCA scores before PFN inference. We theoretically show that rotation makes the column variances nearly equal, so that standardization approximately preserves the embedding geometry. Across image and text classification tasks, encoders, and tabular foundation models, RoFE improves low-data performance over the PCA interface and outperforms baselines that require task-specific training. The improvements also extend to regression.

articles.title: Revealing Geometry under Strong Noise: Spectral Embeddings and Clustering via Random Geometric Graphs
articles.summary: Modern massive datasets often contain useful low-dimensional nonlinear structures that are hidden by noise. Spectral embedding algorithms rely on meaningful local relationships between observations,…
articles.abstract: Modern massive datasets often contain useful low-dimensional nonlinear structures that are hidden by noise. Spectral embedding algorithms rely on meaningful local relationships between observations, but noise accumulated across many coordinates can make the observed distances unreliable. This also complicates clustering when groups have curved or concentric shapes and cannot be distinguished by their centers. In this paper, we develop a new method that denoises pairwise distances before using them to construct spectral embeddings and identify communities. Our approach uses cross-fitted projections to estimate distances between the underlying signals, selects a neighborhood radius from the observed sample, and builds a random geometric graph whose spectral coordinates represent the latent geometric structure. By connecting nearby points, such a geometric graph can distinguish different groups even when their centers coincide. A novel recursive procedure is then proposed to extract clusters from the graph using its spectral embeddings when such clusters exist. On the theoretical side, under a manifold model, we provide guarantees for our spectral embedding algorithm, which can be understood through the eigendecomposition of an integral operator associated with the underlying geometry. We show that the algorithm is robust to noise when the total noise energy is comparable to the total signal energy or, under additional conditions, exceeds it. To our knowledge, this is among the first spectral embedding algorithms that can handle such strong noise in datasets with nonlinear structures. In addition, our proposed clustering algorithm can recover the underlying clusters even when their centers coincide. Numerical studies demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed method in mitigating noise and revealing geometric structures for both spectral embedding and clustering.

articles.title: Prediction-Powered Regression via Calibration: Beyond the Supervised Minimax Benchmark
articles.summary: We study nonparametric regression with limited labeled data and abundant observations carrying potentially inaccurate pseudo-labels. Our proposed method, weighted prediction-powered regression via…
articles.abstract: We study nonparametric regression with limited labeled data and abundant observations carrying potentially inaccurate pseudo-labels. Our proposed method, weighted prediction-powered regression via calibration (wPPRC), first calibrates pseudo-labels using labeled data, then fits a predictor by weighted regression using observed and calibrated responses. Over Hölder classes, we derive nonasymptotic excess-risk bounds for clipped ReLU estimators and establish a minimax lower bound for the corresponding regression problem. Under suitable conditions, the upper and lower bounds match up to logarithmic factors. Moreover, wPPRC can achieve a worst-case risk of smaller order than the minimax risks under four baseline observation structures on the same joint distribution class, demonstrating the value of additional pseudo-labels. We also construct a validation-selected (VS) estimator using an independent labeled validation sample to choose the weight. The VS estimator satisfies an expected-risk oracle inequality and preserves the improvement over the baseline minimax risks with the same total labeled-data budget. Simulations and an application to predicting homeless counts illustrate the gains of the proposed estimators.

articles.title: $K$-Midranks: A robust clustering algorithm for heavy-tailed data with applications to spectroscopy and finance
articles.summary: Clustering data with extreme observations and heavy tails can be challenging for methods that rely on distances between raw observations or specific distributional assumptions. We introduce…
articles.abstract: Clustering data with extreme observations and heavy tails can be challenging for methods that rely on distances between raw observations or specific distributional assumptions. We introduce $K$-midranks, a clustering method that replaces observations with coordinatewise ranks and partitions the transformed data using a procedure analogous to $K$-means. This transformation reduces the influence of extreme values while preserving the ordering of observations within each variable. We evaluate $K$-midranks against $K$-means, $K$-medoids, and mixture models based on Gaussian, Student's t, Cauchy, and generalized hyperbolic distributions through simulation studies, and provide some theoretical properties. $K$-midranks generally outperforms the competing methods on Cauchy-shifted data. In contrast, $K$-means and model-based methods perform better on Gaussian data and Student's t data with three degrees of freedom. We demonstrate the method's practical use in grouping samples based on Raman and LIBS spectra and clustering S\&P 500 stocks according to their returns. $K$-midranks achieves competitive performance with model-based methods in the spectroscopy applications and the best performance among the methods considered in the stock-return application. These findings suggest that $K$-midranks provides a useful alternative for clustering data with Cauchy-like heavy tails. An R package implementing the proposed method is available.

articles.title: Aggregation Rules Induced by KL-Regularised Preference Dynamics on Networks
articles.summary: We study agents that each align a model to their own preference data while observing one another, and ask which aggregation rule the resulting policies implement. Each round, an agent takes one…
articles.abstract: We study agents that each align a model to their own preference data while observing one another, and ask which aggregation rule the resulting policies implement. Each round, an agent takes one KL-regularised step. The step involves a reference that the agent is penalised for leaving and a challenger against which its responses are compared, and each of the two may be the agent's own or an average over the agents it observes; attention need not be reciprocal. Aggregating the reference makes the rule collective. Agent $v$ then has the weight $π_v/β_v$, its share of the network's long-run attention divided by its temperature. If, in addition, the challenger is fixed, the agents concentrate on the response maximising $\sum_v(π_v/β_v)r_v(y)$, where $r_v$ is agent $v$'s reward, and the rule is cardinal. If the reference is fixed and the challenger aggregated, the agents' policies at a fixed point generally differ, and any weighted mean of them is an approximate maximal lottery whatever the weights, so the dynamics select no weighting. If both are aggregated, the rule is ordinal: averaged over rounds, the collective policy is a maximal lottery of the influence-weighted preference kernel, up to a slack that we bound. Where a collective rule exists, its weights depend only on the attention weights and the temperatures.

articles.title: A theory of inductive node-level generalization from a single large graph
articles.summary: In Graph Machine Learning (GML), the notion of generalization fundamentally varies depending on the task level and the properties of the dataset. For instance, graph-level tasks fit into the…
articles.abstract: In Graph Machine Learning (GML), the notion of generalization fundamentally varies depending on the task level and the properties of the dataset. For instance, graph-level tasks fit into the traditional ML framework of i.i.d. samples, with relatively small graphs. On the contrary, node-level tasks involve dependent nodes, often in a few large graphs. Existing studies often consider the transductive settings, where training and test data co-exist in the same graph, or, for inductive learning, try to recover some kind of probabilistic ``independence'', e.g. by still assuming a large number of independent graphs or subgraphs. In this work, we develop a novel framework to express the generalization capabilities of Graph ML algorithms for inductive node-level tasks when learning from a single large graph, taking inspiration from the literature on GNN transferability. In particular, we emphasize the similarities with classical ML by revisiting the excess risk decomposition with a new notion of ``transferable'' risk on large graphs. We apply this framework to Latent Position random graphs: we uncover new insights on the hardness of GML compared to traditional ML, and derive novel notions of concentration. Finally, we apply this framework to several models of GNNs, unifying several existing results on GNNs transferability and universality.

articles.title: Fast and Consistent Structure Learning in Graphical Models via Approximate Cross-Validation
articles.summary: Structure learning for sparse graphical models in high dimensions requires both computational scalability and selection consistency. Classical criteria such as (Extended) Bayesian Information…
articles.abstract: Structure learning for sparse graphical models in high dimensions requires both computational scalability and selection consistency. Classical criteria such as (Extended) Bayesian Information Criterion can provide consistency, but rely on model-specific likelihoods and complexity calibration. In comparison, cross-validation avoids such analytic calibration and is therefore attractive for graph learning. However, cross-validation is computationally infeasible and theoretically inconsistent in structure learning. This creates a tension between consistency and flexibility in modeling. In this work, we resolve the tension by developing a scalable graph-recovery procedure built on approximate cross-validation. We demonstrate its effectiveness in learning large graphical models both theoretically and empirically, and establish selection consistency under mild signal strength assumptions.

articles.title: Precise Asymptotics of Non-Convex M-Estimators
articles.summary: Precise asymptotic theory for M-estimators in high-dimensional settings is largely limited to convex or mildly non-convex formulations, yet non-convex loss functions as well as regularizers are…
articles.abstract: Precise asymptotic theory for M-estimators in high-dimensional settings is largely limited to convex or mildly non-convex formulations, yet non-convex loss functions as well as regularizers are widely used in practice. We study M-estimation in generalized linear models (GLMs) where the loss function or the regularizer can be non-convex. Under rotationally invariant design matrices in the proportional asymptotic regime, we analyze the problem through Vector Approximate Message Passing (VAMP), whose iterates are described by a low-dimensional deterministic recursion called State Evolution (SE). Existing proofs of SE require the proximal operators of the loss function and the regularizer to be Lipschitz, but a non-convex loss or regularizer can have a discontinuous proximal operator, and the usual Onsager terms in VAMP then miss the contribution of the discontinuities. Assuming that the proximal operators are special functions of locally bounded variation, we derive a correction to the Onsager terms using a distributional Stein's lemma. We prove that SE holds for the corrected VAMP. We apply the theory to analyze group sparse regression with an $\ell_0$-type penalty and to robust regression with the Cauchy loss.

articles.title: MTL-MHOL: Predicting Online Conversions under Delayed Feedback and Data Sparsity
articles.summary: This paper proposes the model-agnostic Multi-Task Learning Multi-Head Online Learning (MTL-MHOL) framework for conversion rate (CVR) prediction. Existing approaches typically address key challenges…
articles.abstract: This paper proposes the model-agnostic Multi-Task Learning Multi-Head Online Learning (MTL-MHOL) framework for conversion rate (CVR) prediction. Existing approaches typically address key challenges in CVR prediction, such as delayed feedback and data sparsity, in isolation or lack flexibility and practical applicability. MTL-MHOL adopts a time bucketing approach to account for delayed feedback and combines it with multi-task learning of an auxiliary task to mitigate data sparsity. We evaluate the framework on proprietary datasets from a private company and on a public dataset from Criteo. MTL-MHOL matches or outperforms all benchmark models in terms of Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) and Relative Cross Entropy (RCE), and it correctly captures temporal trends in the data using an MLP backbone, while maintaining strong performance with a DeepFM backbone. In particular, MTL-MHOL matches the performance of the advanced delayed-feedback method FSIW, outperforms the entire-space approach ESMM by 21.5% in RCE, and achieves up to 81% lift in RCE compared to the best-performing classical benchmark.

articles.title: What Environment Invariance Identifies: Minimal Invariant Sets in Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces
articles.summary: Invariant causal prediction identifies the direct causes of a target $Y$ by searching for covariate sets whose conditional law of $Y$ is stable across environments. We state that criterion at the…
articles.abstract: Invariant causal prediction identifies the direct causes of a target $Y$ by searching for covariate sets whose conditional law of $Y$ is stable across environments. We state that criterion at the level of operators, calling a set $S$ invariant when the conditional mean embeddings of $Y$ given $X_S$ agree across environments, and characterise the resulting family exactly: under two conditions on the environments, which we state separately because they fail independently, the invariant sets are precisely those containing $PA(Y)$ and no descendant of $Y$. Two consequences follow. Invariance does not identify $PA(Y)$ uniquely, since every descendant-free superset is invariant as well; and $PA(Y)$ is the unique minimal invariant set. In finite samples, recovery requires the non-invariant sets to be separated from invariance by a margin, and the sample size splits into a screening term logarithmic in the ambient dimension and a term inherited from conditional mean embedding estimation, which is the binding one. The characterisation yields two selection rules with different failure modes, of which the conservative one controls false positives. Controlled experiments verify each population prediction directly, including the failure of uniqueness. They also show that invariance testing is a practical bottleneck: two natural designs are severely miscalibrated, while the selected test reduces but does not eliminate Type I error inflation.

articles.title: SCAN: Neural Additive Networks for Scalable High-Order Component Selection and Estimation
articles.summary: Functional ANOVA models express a prediction as a sum of main effects and interactions, but existing neural functional ANOVA models require the interactions to be specified in advance, which forces a…
articles.abstract: Functional ANOVA models express a prediction as a sum of main effects and interactions, but existing neural functional ANOVA models require the interactions to be specified in advance, which forces a trade-off between missing higher-order structure and the cost of enumerating many interactions. We propose SCAN (Scalable Component Additive Networks), which learns which features each basis function combines, so that components of different orders are selected and estimated jointly without enumerating candidates. The learned component index sets form a small candidate collection on which post-hoc identification is carried out efficiently. A global component-selection parameter shares information across basis functions, and truncating negligible component-selection weights gives a sparse model that is identified after training. We establish universal approximation, a minimax optimal rate up to a logarithmic factor, and component selection consistency, which together imply that the discovered components contain all identified true components with probability tending to one. In synthetic experiments, SCAN learns components whose maximum order is close to the true one, and recovers higher-order components more accurately than the baseline models, with post-hoc identification taking a few seconds for 100 inputs. SCAN also outperforms most neural functional ANOVA models in prediction on the benchmark datasets and trains at a much lower cost than exhaustive second-order models. We also apply SCAN to predict treatment response in breast cancer from 12,502 gene-expression variables.

articles.title: Does coverage explain core-set active learning? Mean, max, and the choice of distance
articles.summary: Core-set selection casts batch active learning as a covering problem, in which the points to label minimise the covering radius of the pool. Its main argument is a generalization bound in which this…
articles.abstract: Core-set selection casts batch active learning as a covering problem, in which the points to label minimise the covering radius of the pool. Its main argument is a generalization bound in which this radius controls the gap between the loss on the pool and on the labelled sample. We examine what this bound requires and what it says in practice. We first state it with the assumption that its proof uses at the labelled points, a zero conditional risk, and show that it then holds for any dissimilarity and any selection rule that uses no label outside the sample. The proof works point by point and involves two averages, the mean distance of the pool to the labelled sample and the purity of the cells attached to the labelled points. Keeping them gives, when labels are deterministic at the labelled points, a bound on the pool loss with no zero-loss assumption and without the factor C, the number of classes, of the original constant. We then compare scales, for deterministic labels and a regression function Lipschitz on the whole pool. With the original constant, the bound can be informative only if the radius is below the smallest distance between two classes divided by C. Without C, its radius form can be informative only once the nearest-neighbour rule built on the sample is exact on the pool. Finally, a misalignment criterion measures whether a quantity ranks selections as the gap or the test error do. Experiments on a Gaussian pool and on two image pools, digits and MNIST, the latter under eight distances, and with a network retrained at each cycle, show that the radius does not rank selections consistently with the gap and, on the image pools, that the bounds that do not use the labels of the pool are never informative and that covering in mean rather than in maximum, as greedy k-medoids does, gives a higher purity and accuracy than random sampling.

articles.title: Spectral Regularization Beyond Ridge Regression
articles.summary: We study Inclusive Ridge (IR), a two-parameter spectral regularization family that contains ridge regression as well as iterated Tikhonov regularization. We derive its exact finite-sample coefficient…
articles.abstract: We study Inclusive Ridge (IR), a two-parameter spectral regularization family that contains ridge regression as well as iterated Tikhonov regularization. We derive its exact finite-sample coefficient risk and establish necessary and sufficient conditions for increasing or decreasing the additional filter-shape parameter around the ridge baseline to locally lower risk. We show that oracle-tuned ridge is generically suboptimal within the IR family. Under joint divergence of the penalty and filter order, we show that a nondegenerate spectral limit exists precisely when their ratio converges to a positive finite constant, yielding a continuous exponential filter. Along the fixed effective-scale path, we also obtain an exact risk-difference comparison and explicit sufficient conditions under which both higher-order estimators and the exponential limiting filter strictly outperform oracle-tuned ridge. In this regime, IR becomes progressively less sensitive to perturbations in the absolute penalty parameter while retaining sensitivity to its effective spectral scale, and a plug-in coefficient-risk first-order condition coincides with a degrees-of-freedom-adjusted discrepancy equation. Numerical examples based on the Fredholm inverse problem, tomographic reconstruction, a regression design, and synthetic difference-in-differences donor-weight estimation illustrate both the potential gains and the limitations of feasible tuning, distinguishing oracle improvements from gains attainable with estimated tuning parameters.

articles.title: Tensor Recovery with Heterogeneous Mode Structures
articles.summary: Tensor recovery methods often impose a common structural assumption across modes, even when different modes may exhibit distinct forms of regularity. We propose a unified convex framework that treats…
articles.abstract: Tensor recovery methods often impose a common structural assumption across modes, even when different modes may exhibit distinct forms of regularity. We propose a unified convex framework that treats each mode according to its structure. Smoothly varying modes form an indexing domain and are handled by local kernel weighting, whereas retained modes may receive low-rank, group-sparse, graph-Laplacian, or autoregressive regularization in distinct and potentially overlapping combinations. The framework also covers ordinary tensor recovery without local smoothing. A consensus HM-ADMM algorithm separates the active penalties into tractable proximal and linear-system updates. For the population-quadratic estimator, we derive deterministic oracle inequalities and high-probability bounds under independent trace regression. The bounds disentangle stochastic error, rank and support complexity, smoothing bias, and quadratic mismatch. They also identify when quadratic penalties sharpen the Frobenius-error bound. For regular smooth domains, the theory characterizes the bias-variance trade-off and yields an optimal bandwidth order, with a specialization to uniform tensor completion. Simulations and two applications illustrate the gains from matching regularization to mode-specific structure, especially under severe undersampling.

articles.title: Low-Rank Tensor Representations for Efficient Multimarginal Optimal Transport
articles.summary: Multimarginal Optimal Transport (MOT) suffers from exponential computational and memory costs in the number of marginals, as transport plans are represented by high-dimensional tensors. We introduce…
articles.abstract: Multimarginal Optimal Transport (MOT) suffers from exponential computational and memory costs in the number of marginals, as transport plans are represented by high-dimensional tensors. We introduce Low-Rank Multimarginal Optimal Transport (LRMOT), which restricts transport plans to tensors with bounded multilinear rank, providing a compact and structured representation of multimarginal couplings. This structure enables efficient algorithms with a low memory footprint. We establish approximation bounds for the resulting low-rank formulations and demonstrate experimentally that the proposed algorithms substantially reduce computational time while achieving solutions with low transport cost.

articles.title: Boosting zero-shot learning through neuro-symbolic integration
articles.summary: Zero-shot learning (ZSL) aims to train deep neural networks to recognize objects from unseen classes, starting from a semantic description of the concepts. Neuro-symbolic (NeSy) integration refers to…
articles.abstract: Zero-shot learning (ZSL) aims to train deep neural networks to recognize objects from unseen classes, starting from a semantic description of the concepts. Neuro-symbolic (NeSy) integration refers to a class of techniques that incorporate symbolic knowledge representation and reasoning with the learning capabilities of deep neural networks. However, to date, few studies have explored how to leverage NeSy techniques to inject prior knowledge during the training process to boost ZSL capabilities. Here, we present Fuzzy Logic Prototypical Network (FLPN) that formulates the classification task as prototype matching in a visual-semantic embedding space, which is trained by optimizing a NeSy loss. Specifically, FLPN exploits the Logic Tensor Network (LTN) framework to incorporate background knowledge in the form of logical axioms by grounding a first-order logic language as differentiable operations between real tensors. This prior knowledge includes class hierarchies (classes and macroclasses) along with robust high-level inductive biases. The latter allow, for instance, to handle exceptions in class-level attributes and to enforce similarity between images of the same class, preventing premature overfitting to seen classes and improving overall performance. % CHECK: original sentence had no verb ("Both class-level and attribute-level prototypes through an attention mechanism ...") FLPN learns both class-level and attribute-level prototypes, the latter through an attention mechanism specialized for either convolutional- or transformer-based backbones. FLPN achieves state-of-the-art performance on the GZSL benchmarks AWA2 and SUN, matching or exceeding the performance of competing algorithms with minimal computational overhead. The code is available at https://github.com/FrancescoManigrass/FLPN

articles.title: How long must an honest confidence interval be after causal discovery? Benign and malignant weak edges
articles.summary: After causal discovery, a confidence interval for a total effect valid uniformly over the model class must pay for structural uncertainty. We measure this price by the worst-case ratio of expected…
articles.abstract: After causal discovery, a confidence interval for a total effect valid uniformly over the model class must pay for structural uncertainty. We measure this price by the worst-case ratio of expected length to that of the efficient interval knowing the graph, for linear Gaussian models with a known superset of the adjacencies and k-triangle faithfulness. The global price is of order sqrt(n) once one edge can be malignant, so we study it locally, near a generic distribution with one edge absent. Our main result classifies this weak edge by Meek closures. It is benign if deleting it leaves the effect identifiable in the resulting MPDAG and Markov equivalent explanations agree; the local price is then bounded, and otherwise, for small k, of order sqrt(n). At benign edges the price is of order R+K, with R a ratio of efficient lengths and K a cross-model constant. It equals one, so that honesty is free, exactly when K = 0, generically decided by a d-separation. For two Markov classes it is determined within a factor 3.40, and its upper bound is approached without knowing the base point or the weak edge. A further graphical condition gives the rate uniformly in a second edge's margin.

articles.title: Operator-Valued Q-Learning: Compositional Bellman Recursions for Order-Sensitive Decision Making
articles.summary: In quantum pulse sequences, spacecraft attitude control and in-hand reorientation, actions act on a hidden physical state as non-commuting operators, so the outcome of a plan depends on the order of…
articles.abstract: In quantum pulse sequences, spacecraft attitude control and in-hand reorientation, actions act on a hidden physical state as non-commuting operators, so the outcome of a plan depends on the order of its actions. We let the value function carry this structure: each Q(s,a) is an N x N operator, and the Bellman backup applies the action's dual map to the continuation value, Q(s,a) = K_a^*(R(s,a) + gamma E V(s')). Unrolled along a plan, the recursion builds the ordered product of the actions' operators, and the value at any latent state is a linear trace readout. It is exact for policies that do not observe the latent, the backup contracts for unitary and orthogonal dynamics, and an asynchronous operator TD scheme learns it with almost-sure convergence. Classical values live in a lattice, so a maximum over actions exists; self-adjoint operators form an anti-lattice (Kadison) and have none. An operator log-sum-exp still gives one operator per state-action pair whose readout upper-bounds the value of every policy at every latent state. The sampled update converges to it for a finite horizon, and it reduces to soft Q-learning and the QMDP bound when actions commute. We prove that scalar values on observations that ignore action order must confuse swapped histories, that exact history tables grow exponentially for free action groups but polynomially for nilpotent ones, and give a Hankel-rank lower bound on the operator dimension. In experiments the learned policy matches 1000-simulation tree search on SO(3) pointing for horizons up to 20 at ~10^4 times lower decision cost, transfers zero-shot to unseen initial states, and acts exactly on its belief mean when the initial state is hidden, where plugging the mean into a DQN does not. A planner with the same model knowledge is more sample-efficient at short horizons, and a DQN given the operators matches or exceeds OpQ.

articles.title: Revisiting Continual Learning in Language Models: A Three-Interface Diagnosis of Stability and Plasticity
articles.summary: Continual learning in language models is commonly studied in the incremental learning (IL) setting, where a model learns a sequence of tasks and is evaluated through its final classifier or…
articles.abstract: Continual learning in language models is commonly studied in the incremental learning (IL) setting, where a model learns a sequence of tasks and is evaluated through its final classifier or language-model (LM) head. This interface, however, does not indicate where forgetting occurs: a drop in accuracy may reflect representation degradation in the backbone, readout mismatch in the head, or both. We therefore argue that backward transfer (BWT) and forward transfer (FWT) should be interpreted as interface-dependent quantities rather than as single modellevel properties. We study three evaluation interfaces: the trained head, which is updated sequentially with the backbone; a probe newly trained on frozen backbone features; and a classifier-free backbone diagnostic. They measure deployed performance, recoverability under a new readout, and representation separability, respectively. Across class-incremental experiments with encoder and decoder language backbones, plus task-incremental sanity checks, conclusions about forgetting and plasticity change with the interface: the trained head often indicates severe forgetting, the probe near-complete recoverability, and the backbone diagnostic intermediate representation drift with a consistent negative relation between stability and plasticity. This relation holds for clustering-free diagnostics such as nearest-class-mean accuracy and across five clustering algorithms and three metrics. Finally, Just LM-Head Tuning (JLT), a head-only intervention on a fixed incrementally trained backbone, recovers 96-99% of the gap to joint training for replayand distillation-based methods but only about three quarters for plain sequential fine-tuning, suggesting that many failures attributed to catastrophic forgetting reflect head-backbone mismatch plus partial representation drift. Our results call for reporting where forgetting is measured, not only how much.

articles.title: Sparse Hodge Preference Optimization: Fine-Tuning Language Models toward Alignment beyond Transitive Preferences
articles.summary: The growing adoption of Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), which leverages pairwise preference data, reflects its great success in fine-tuning large language models to align with human…
articles.abstract: The growing adoption of Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), which leverages pairwise preference data, reflects its great success in fine-tuning large language models to align with human expectations. It directly optimizes the policy from human preferences without explicit reward modeling or the complexities of reinforcement learning-based approaches. However, the classic DPO relies on the Bradley--Terry sampling model and cannot effectively capture intransitivity or cyclic structures in aggregated human preference data. In this article, we propose Sparse Hodge Preference Optimization (SHPO), a preference optimization algorithm that augments DPO with a sparse antisymmetric curl residual motivated by the combinatorial Hodge decomposition. We prove that SHPO strictly enlarges DPO's hypothesis class on comparison graphs containing at least one triangle, under some mild regularity conditions on the response representations. We further establish a theoretical guarantee for $\ell_1$-regularized estimation of the curl coefficients under fixed policy and representations. Qualitative studies on three preference datasets under the same QLoRA budget, SHPO-aligned LLM achieves satisfactory performances in preference accuracy, cyclic structure recovery, and GPT-4o-judged generation quality.

articles.title: PsyDrift: Healthy-Reference Latent Diffusion for Anomaly Scoring in Autism Spectrum Disorder
articles.summary: Individual heterogeneity and acquisition-site variability complicate neuroimaging-based characterization of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). We propose PsyDrift, combining…
articles.abstract: Individual heterogeneity and acquisition-site variability complicate neuroimaging-based characterization of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). We propose PsyDrift, combining ASD/healthy-control-supervised functional-connectivity representations with healthy-reference latent diffusion. An encoder produces 128-dimensional representations, and a denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) learns exclusively from healthy training latents. Distance from a diffusion-denoised reconstruction provides a continuous deviation score. We evaluate 1,102 subjects from all 20 ABIDE-I sites using five-seed leave-one-site-out cross-validation. The classifier and DDPM achieve mean-site AUROCs of $0.798 \pm 0.003$ and $0.718 \pm 0.013$, respectively; uncertainties denote seed standard deviations. Matched healthy-reference scorers on the same representation achieve 0.68-0.71; the statistical significance of diffusion's modest numerical advantage remains unestablished. Within ASD, scores show weak associations with ADOS Total (Spearman $ρ= 0.108$, $p = 0.038$) and full-scale IQ ($ρ= -0.138$, $p = 0.002$), without adjustment for age, sex, site, or head motion. Frozen evaluation without retraining or hyperparameter adaptation yields pooled AUROCs of 0.69 on ABIDE-II and 0.61 on ADHD-200, providing preliminary evidence of cross-cohort and cross-disorder transfer. These results demonstrate healthy-reference deviation scoring within an ASD-supervised representation; incremental predictive and clinical value remains unestablished.

articles.title: The response field approach to path integral control
articles.summary: This paper investigates non-linear path integral control problems within the response field formalism of nonequilibrium field theory. The aim of this work is exploratory, based on the identification…
articles.abstract: This paper investigates non-linear path integral control problems within the response field formalism of nonequilibrium field theory. The aim of this work is exploratory, based on the identification of correspondences between backward adjoint processes and the response field of non-equilibrium statistical physics, whose properties have not been set out in an optimal control setting. The response field is found to play an analogous role to the backward adjoint process under the stochastic maximum principle. In particular, the gradient of the optimal cost-to-go at the initial time, which is proportional to the optimal control, is given by the average of the response field at the initial time. In contrast to the case of non-equilibrium dynamics, the response function is found to be acausal in the control setting. The linear-quadratic case of path integral control is studied, confirming it as the free theory, meaning that solving the control problem is equivalent to completing the square and determining the propagator for a two point boundary value problem. The developments presented here are a necessary prelude to applications based on field theoretic approximation, for both path integral control and their dual inference problems.

articles.title: Sequential Selection against an Adaptive Opponent
articles.summary: Selecting a strategy by testing it against an opponent is common in game-playing AI, red-teaming of language models, and safety evaluations of AI agents. In many of these settings, the opponent…
articles.abstract: Selecting a strategy by testing it against an opponent is common in game-playing AI, red-teaming of language models, and safety evaluations of AI agents. In many of these settings, the opponent adapts to what it observes, so a strategy that keeps winning in practice may already have stopped working by the time it is used. Motivated by these settings, we study a player who tries strategies in practice games against an adaptive opponent, decides when to stop, and then either selects one strategy for the next game or abstains. The goal is to select a strategy that meets a target win probability while rarely selecting one that has already fallen below it. For a single strategy, we propose the Sequential Private Accumulated-excess Rule (SPAR), which accumulates evidence through a capped likelihood ratio and selects the strategy once this evidence reaches a privately drawn uniform threshold. We show that the stopping time must involve such private randomness. The number of games SPAR needs is inversely proportional to the error tolerance, and this rate is optimal even when the opponent happens not to adapt. To select among multiple strategies, we introduce Screen-then-SPAR, which screens candidates in stages before applying SPAR. The procedure adapts to the best strategy's unknown initial margin above the target and achieves the minimax rate up to logarithmic factors. The performance of Screen-then-SPAR is demonstrated through simulations and two real-data studies, one using recorded coding-agent attacks from MonitoringBench and the other using rock-paper-scissors matches between human players and an adaptive bot.

articles.title: Training Dynamics of Large State-Transition Models
articles.summary: Next-token prediction relies on learned token embeddings whose dimension $d$ is much smaller than the vocabulary size $V$. Existing analyses of training dynamics either fix the embeddings with $d\ge…
articles.abstract: Next-token prediction relies on learned token embeddings whose dimension $d$ is much smaller than the vocabulary size $V$. Existing analyses of training dynamics either fix the embeddings with $d\ge V$ or train them only in restricted settings. It remains unclear whether jointly training the embeddings by gradient-based methods from random initialization leads to accurate prediction when $d<V$. In this paper, we study this question in the simplest setting where it is already nontrivial, namely next-token prediction with a one-token context, which we refer to as a state-transition model. The model consists of an input embedding and an output embedding, either untied or tied, and is trained from Gaussian initialization by perturbed gradient descent with weight decay on the population cross-entropy loss. We consider ground-truth transition laws whose centered log-probability table has low rank and bounded entries, and measure the prediction quality by the relative prediction gain (RPG). It is zero for the uniform predictor and one for the optimal predictor. For the untied model, we show that when $d=Ω(\sqrt V)$, with probability at least $1-e^{-cd}$ for some constant $c$, the RPG is above $7/8$ at every iterate in the final $1-1/d$ fraction of training iterations. For the tied model trained on a subset of states, we prove that the RPG on the observed states is $1-O(V/d^2)$, and under a coverage condition on the ground truth and a bound on the learned embeddings, we further prove a prediction guarantee on the unseen states.
